segments.title: Leaving New Orleans for Chicago in 1926
segments.summary: Williams says he moved to Chicago at 19; his father, a contractor, could not get into the union and went back, as did his mother in the 1930s. He travelled free on the railroad.

segments.title: New Orleans piano players: Udell Wilson
segments.summary: Asked about unrecorded New Orleans barrelhouse pianists, he names Steve Lewis and Udell Wilson, a long-fingered Kansas City player who worked the downtown joints in the 1920s.

segments.title: Red Cayou and his brother Yellow
segments.summary: He recalls Red Cayou, who left New Orleans for Oakland, stopped playing and died there, and Red's brother Yellow, who also played.

segments.title: Little Willie and the unrecorded New Orleans pianists
segments.summary: Little Willie and Red held jam sessions; these men played everything with a strong left hand like a whole band, and none got to record. Terry Wilson took some of their style.

segments.title: New Orleans as a piano town: solo work in the joints
segments.summary: Before pianos were used in bands, pianists played alone in the joints as entertainment.

segments.title: Younger players and more names: Santiago, Joe Robichaux, Stackelia
segments.summary: They compare ages and go over more New Orleans names, including the Santiagos, Joe Robichaux, Charlie Hampton and Stackelia, whom Williams knew in the 1920s.

segments.chapter: Starting out in New Orleans and Chicago
segments.title: Being younger than Armstrong and Lee Collins, too young for the joints
segments.summary: Williams says Armstrong and Lee Collins were older than he and he came up under them. In New Orleans he could play only school events and was kept out of the joints.

segments.chapter: Starting out in New Orleans and Chicago
segments.title: A 1946 photograph, and playing pop tunes as well as blues
segments.summary: Looking at a photo of a group, Williams says he played swing and pop, not just blues. He again says he could not play in the New Orleans places in his day.

segments.chapter: Starting out in New Orleans and Chicago
segments.title: First years in Chicago: ten years as a solo pianist in roadhouses
segments.summary: He started playing in Chicago in 1926, working as a solo pianist for ten years in gangster roadhouses and speakeasies, including Cicero.

segments.chapter: Starting out in New Orleans and Chicago
segments.title: Playing with Jimmy Bertrand in a trio, 1939-40
segments.summary: Williams played in a three-piece group with drummer Jimmy Bertrand and Chris Richell in 1939-40, during the depression.

segments.chapter: Starting out in New Orleans and Chicago
segments.title: Sitting in with Bebe Ridgley's band as a New Orleans teenager
segments.summary: As a teenager Williams was fetched to sit in with William Ridgley's Tuxedo band. Ridgley encouraged him in music and gave him clarinet lessons.

segments.chapter: Starting out in New Orleans and Chicago
segments.title: Playing a concert with Bunk Johnson in Chicago
segments.summary: Asked about Bunk Johnson and George Lewis, Williams says he played with Bunk, who hung out at his place while in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Starting out in New Orleans and Chicago
segments.title: Photographs of Bebe Ridgley after his stroke
segments.summary: Looking at pictures of Bebe Ridgley, Williams describes him as a proud, fine man who had a stroke late in life and drank.

segments.title: Barrelhouse names from the interviewer's list: Clayton, Dookie, Honey
segments.summary: The interviewer reads names of piano players; Williams knows only Clayton (piano and trumpet) and says others came after he left. He recalls Honey and Little Willie.

segments.chapter: Starting out in New Orleans and Chicago
segments.title: First professional job with Chris Kelly and Sweet Black in New Orleans
segments.summary: Williams played with Chris Kelly in a piano, trumpet and drums trio for Sweet Black on Franklin Street, his first professional work, with drummer Papa Crutcher.

segments.chapter: Starting out in New Orleans and Chicago
segments.title: Filling in for Ridgley as a teenage neighbor
segments.summary: Ridgley, who lived on his street, would come for him when a pianist did not show up, and his mother did not mind.

segments.title: Playing the Clark Street honky tonks with Herb Morand
segments.summary: In Chicago he played with Herb Morand in three-piece combos at the Firehouse and Lawrence O'Brien's joint on Clark Street.

segments.title: The Lake Michigan excursion boats and the drummer Tom
segments.summary: He played on the North Shore excursion boat. The pay was a dollar plus $16-17 a night in tips. Tom, a New Orleans musician, later quit for the steel mill.

segments.title: Hard times for musicians in the 1940s
segments.summary: Musicians earned little through the depression and early 1940s. Things only boomed after World War II.

segments.title: Being drafted in 1940 with Morand and Horace Malcolm
segments.summary: Williams registered in the first draft with Herb Morand, Horace Malcolm and Tom Taylor but did not serve because he had six dependent children.

segments.title: How the dance boats worked and what they paid
segments.summary: He explains the boats ran a quarter-a-dance cruise from downtown to Jackson Park, and the band played hard to draw people on, earning $16-17 a night.

segments.title: Ten years with Lee Collins's combo
segments.summary: Williams says he worked mostly with trumpeter Lee Collins, piano and trumpet, from wartime until about 1950-51.

segments.title: Jeep Robinson, now an insurance agent
segments.summary: He identifies a second trumpeter as Jeep Robinson, who played with Paul Barbarin in Chicago and now writes insurance.

segments.title: Willie Mabel, the blues pianist Jeep recorded with
segments.summary: Williams recalls piano player Willie Mabel, who recorded with Jeep. He judges him limited, with every song alike.

segments.title: Boogie-woogie players in Chicago in the late 1920s
segments.summary: Asked about boogie players, Williams says there are none left now. Jimmy Yancey and Lucky Lewis are mentioned.

segments.title: Arnold Wiley, the Arkansas pianist
segments.summary: Williams describes Wiley, from Arkansas, as a superb pianist who played everything and who came to Chicago in the late 1920s. He recalls his song about 35th and State.

segments.title: Helping Wiley sell his records door to door
segments.summary: Williams helped Wiley sell his 1928 Brunswick records at houses and in bootleg places, playing piano to sell them.

segments.title: Wiley and Wiley, and seeing him in the Chicago Defender
segments.summary: He recalls Wiley's wife, who danced and sang, and the Wiley and Wiley billing. Years later he saw Wiley's picture in the Chicago Defender, from Detroit.

segments.title: Charlie Spence and Chuck Seager, who played with Joe Oliver
segments.summary: They discuss pianist Chuck Seager, from Monroe, Louisiana, who played with Joe Oliver in Chicago in the early 1920s and recorded with him.

segments.title: Quick right hand, and playing the clarinet part
segments.summary: Williams says his fingers are slow now but he had a quick right hand and played the clarinet part on the piano.

segments.title: Playing only the black keys: Bugus and Irving Berlin
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about a pianist named Bugus who played only black keys. Williams says Irving Berlin did the same.

segments.title: Playing an old New Orleans blues
segments.summary: Williams plays an old blues from New Orleans and the interviewer asks to restart the recording.

segments.title: The Poor Buddy Richard blues and Aaron Harris
segments.summary: He says the piece is the Poor Buddy Richard blues, about a killing by the bad man Aaron Harris. He played it with Lee Collins and says it can be done slow or jump style.

segments.title: Closing playing and tape noise
segments.summary: The last blocks are mostly garbled ASR from piano playing and thanks.
